title: Did Israel always believe in one God?
question: Was ancient Israel monotheistic from the time of Moses, or did belief in one God emerge over centuries out of a world full of gods? And how should we read biblical texts that mention other 'gods'?
intro:
The Bible ends with a clear confession that there is one God and that idols are nothing (1 Cor 8:4-6). But the Old Testament also speaks of 'gods' in ways that surprise modern readers: Yahweh is praised as greater than 'all gods' (Ps 95:3), stands in a 'divine assembly' (Ps 82:1), and in one ancient form of Deut 32:8 divides the nations by the number of the 'sons of God'. The prophets condemn Israelites who worshipped Baal, Asherah and the Queen of Heaven, and archaeology has found Hebrew inscriptions that bless people 'by Yahweh and his asherah'.

So how did Israel get from there to the confession 'there is no God besides me' (Isa 45:5)? Four main answers are on the table. Classical monotheism says Israel's faith was monotheistic in principle from Moses, and the other gods are either idols or Israel's own apostasy. Divine-council monotheism says Yahweh was always unique and supreme, but the Bible really does speak of other created spiritual beings called elohim. Evolutionary monotheism says Israel's religion grew out of Canaanite religion and only became fully monotheistic around the exile. The 'Yahweh-alone' view says a determined minority party fought the popular, many-gods religion for centuries and finally won.

These views overlap: almost everyone agrees that many ordinary Israelites worshipped other gods, and almost everyone agrees that the later books teach that Yahweh alone is God. The debate is about what was there at the start, what the 'gods' language means, and whether the biblical story of a faithful core and an unfaithful majority is basically right.

positions.name: Classical monotheism (from Moses)
positions.summary:
On this view, Israel's faith was monotheistic in principle from the time of Moses. The God who brought Israel out of Egypt is the Creator of heaven and earth, and he alone is to be worshipped (Exod 20:3; Deut 6:4). Texts that mention other 'gods' are either poetic comparisons, references to idols that the nations wrongly honoured, or descriptions of angels and human rulers who carry delegated authority. Israel's long history of idolatry is real, but the Bible tells it as apostasy from a faith Israel already had, not as the slow birth of that faith.

In its scholarly form, associated above all with Yehezkel Kaufmann, the argument is that Israel's religion was a new kind of religion. Pagan gods are born, mate, fight and die, and are subject to fate and magic; Israel's God has no birth, no consort and no myth, and stands outside nature. Kaufmann argued that biblical writers barely understood real paganism, mocking idols as wood and stone (Isa 44:9-20), which suggests a long-standing monotheistic culture rather than one just emerging from polytheism. Many evangelical scholars hold a similar view on both historical and theological grounds.

positions.context: The view is the traditional reading in Judaism and Christianity, taken for granted until the nineteenth century. It was restated in the twentieth century against Julius Wellhausen's late dating of Israel's law and against comparative studies that made Israel one more Near Eastern religion. Kaufmann gave it a critical-scholarly form; Albright and his students supported it from archaeology; evangelical scholars continue it today, often while accepting that the Bible uses 'gods' language for angels or idols.
claims: The God of Moses is the one Creator; the first commandment and the Shema assume and demand that Israel worship no other (Exod 20:3; Deut 6:4).
Deuteronomy already states that there is no other God in heaven or on earth (Deut 4:35; Deut 4:39), so explicit monotheism is not first invented in the exile.
Biblical 'gods' language is mostly comparative or polemical: the gods are idols, or angels and rulers under God's authority.
The idolatry described in Judges, Kings and the prophets is apostasy from an earlier covenant faith, not evidence that the faith did not yet exist.
Israel's God differs in kind from the pagan gods: no birth, no consort, no death, no dependence on magic or fate.

scriptures.reading: 'No other gods before me' is given at Sinai as the foundation of the covenant.
Israel was shown signs so that it would know that the LORD is God and there is none else besides him.
The Shema confesses the one LORD and calls for undivided love.
God creates heaven and earth alone, with no rival or battle, in contrast to Near Eastern creation myths.
God is first and last; besides him there is no God, and he challenges any rival to speak.
The nations have changed gods 'which are yet no gods' while Israel has forsaken the true God.

arguments.text: The Pentateuch and Joshua present exclusive Yahweh worship as the original covenant demand, renewed in each generation (Josh 24:14-24).
The prophets accuse Israel of abandoning an older faith, appealing to the exodus and wilderness as a time of first love (Jer 2:2; Hos 11:1-2). They do not present themselves as innovators.

Biblical polemic against idols treats them as mere objects (Isa 44:9-20). Kaufmann argued this shows a culture so long monotheistic that it no longer understood how pagans thought of the god behind the image.
Israel's God has no consort and no myth of birth or death in the biblical texts, even early poems, which is unusual for the period and suggests a distinct religion from the start.

critiques.text: Inscriptions such as Kuntillet Ajrud and Khirbet el-Qom, female figurines found in Judahite homes, and the prophets' own complaints suggest that worship of other gods was normal and widespread, not a fringe apostasy.
Texts like Ps 82, Deut 32:8 (Qumran reading) and Ps 89:5-7 really do describe other divine beings; turning them all into human judges or poetic figures is strained.

The passages that state monotheism most clearly (Deut 4; Isa 40–48) are dated by most critical scholars to the late monarchy or exile, so citing them for Moses assumes an early date that many dispute.

responses.text: The Bible itself says most Israelites often worshipped other gods (Judg 2:11-13; Jer 11:13). Archaeology confirms the biblical description of popular religion; it does not show what the covenant faith required.
Many classical monotheists accept that angels are called 'gods' or 'sons of God' and see no conflict: they are creatures under God's rule, so the core claim stands.
Dating is itself debated, and the demand for exclusive loyalty in early texts such as Exod 15 and the Decalogue already points toward monotheism even before it is put in philosophical terms.

strawMen.strawMan: Classical monotheists deny that Israelites ever worshipped other gods.
strawMen.correction: They insist that they did, constantly, because the Bible says so. The disagreement is whether this was departure from an existing faith.

strawMen.strawMan: This view ignores archaeology.
strawMen.correction: Kaufmann, Albright and later defenders engaged closely with Ugarit and Near Eastern texts; they read the evidence as popular religion rather than official faith.

positive: Takes the Bible's own story of covenant and apostasy seriously as history.
Keeps a clear line between the Creator and every creature, the basis of Jewish and Christian worship.
negative: Can flatten texts that genuinely speak of heavenly beings, explaining them away too quickly.
Can underplay how deeply Israel's culture shared the religious world of its neighbours.

positions.name: Divine-council monotheism (Yahweh unique among created elohim)
positions.summary:
This view says the Bible teaches that Yahweh alone is God in the full sense: uncreated, all-powerful, Creator of everything else. But it also takes at face value texts that speak of other heavenly beings called elohim, 'gods' or 'sons of God', who meet in his council (Ps 82:1; Ps 89:5-7; Job 1:6). These beings are created and subordinate. Some were given oversight of the nations (Deut 32:8-9, following the Qumran reading), rebelled, and became the powers behind the nations' gods. So the Bible is not polytheistic, but its monotheism is not the modern idea that no other spiritual beings exist.

Michael Heiser popularised the slogan that Yahweh is an elohim but no other elohim is Yahweh. 'Elohim' names a kind of being who lives in the spiritual realm, not a set of divine attributes; the dead Samuel (1 Sam 28:13) and Chemosh (Judg 11:24) can be called elohim too. Richard Bauckham's related idea of 'divine identity' argues that Jews of Jesus' day defined the one God by what only he does (creates all things and rules all things) rather than by denying that angels exist. On this reading, Jesus is included in that unique identity in the New Testament (1 Cor 8:6).

positions.context: Interest in the divine council grew after the Ugaritic texts (found from 1929) showed a council of El with 'sons of El' meeting on a mountain. H. Wheeler Robinson (1944), Frank Moore Cross (1973) and Mullen (1980) studied the biblical parallels, mostly within a developmental framework. Heiser took the same evidence and argued that it fits a consistent, high view of Yahweh across the canon. The model spread widely in evangelical circles after *The Unseen Realm*, especially through podcasts and the BibleProject's teaching on spiritual beings.
claims: Elohim is a word for a class of spiritual beings; Yahweh is the unique, uncreated elohim and Creator of the rest.
God presides over a council of created divine beings (sons of God) who take part in his rule (1 Kgs 22:19-23; Job 1:6; Ps 89:5-7).
After Babel, the nations were placed under these beings while Yahweh kept Israel as his portion (Deut 32:8-9; Deut 4:19).
Some council members rebelled and misruled the nations; God judges them (Ps 82) and in Christ reclaims the nations (Col 2:15).
'None besides me' texts declare Yahweh's incomparability and sole deity in the full sense, not the non-existence of other spirits.

scriptures.reading: God takes his stand in the divine assembly and judges among the gods.
Yahweh is feared in the council of the holy ones; none among the sons of the mighty is like him.
With the Qumran reading, the nations are allotted by the number of the sons of God, but Jacob is the LORD's own portion.
Micaiah sees the host of heaven around the throne, discussing how to bring about Ahab's fall.
The LORD is 'God of gods, and Lord of lords', supreme over the whole category.
There are 'so-called gods' and 'many gods and many lords', yet for us one God and one Lord.

arguments.text: Council texts are spread across the Law, Psalms, Prophets and Writings, and the New Testament speaks of thrones, rulers and authorities (Col 1:16; Eph 6:12). A view that explains them together is preferable to many separate explanations.

Paul says idols are nothing, yet that sacrifices to them go to demons (1 Cor 10:19-21), echoing Deut 32:17. The Bible itself holds 'no other gods in Yahweh's class' together with 'real spiritual powers exist'.
The Dead Sea Scrolls reading of Deut 32:8 ('sons of God'), supported by the Septuagint, is now accepted by many textual critics and translations (ESV, NRSV), which strengthens the council reading.
If 'elohim' meant 'possessing all divine attributes', calling the dead Samuel an elohim (1 Sam 28:13) would make no sense. So the word must name a kind of being, not a rank equal to Yahweh.

critiques.text: Second Isaiah and Deuteronomy go further than 'incomparable': they say other gods are nothing and cannot act (Isa 41:23-24; Isa 44:9). Calling angels 'gods' imports a category Christians have usually avoided.

Reading every council text as part of one consistent system ignores evidence that the texts come from different periods, and that some (such as the older form of Deut 32:8) picture Yahweh as one of El's sons rather than the Most High himself.

The model sometimes builds large conclusions (territorial spirits, a detailed three-rebellion story) on a few texts and on Second Temple writings like 1 Enoch, and popular versions can encourage speculation about spiritual geography.

responses.text: Isaiah also uses the 'none besides me' formula for Babylon (Isa 47:8, 10), where it plainly means 'no rival'. Denying that idols have power does not require denying that any spiritual beings exist, which Isaiah elsewhere affirms (Isa 6:1-3).
Even if older traditions existed, the canonical text identifies Yahweh with Elyon and El (Gen 14:22; Ps 97:9). The model reads the final form, which is what churches and synagogues use.
Careful defenders separate what the Bible states from what Second Temple writers added, and mark speculative points. Abuse in popular teaching does not refute the core exegesis.

strawMen.strawMan: The divine council view is polytheism dressed up.
strawMen.correction: It explicitly teaches one uncreated God who made all other spirits and alone deserves worship. Its claim is about what other beings exist, not about worshipping them.

strawMen.strawMan: This is Heiser's invention.
strawMen.correction: The council reading of Ps 82 and Deut 32:8 is old (it appears in Second Temple texts and the Septuagint) and was argued by many mainstream scholars before him; Heiser's contribution was a whole-Bible synthesis.

positive: Makes sense of puzzling texts that many readers skip, and links Old Testament and New Testament language about powers.
Gives a clear story of mission: the nations are being reclaimed from rebel powers in Christ.
negative: Popular versions can fuel speculation about territorial demons and hidden spiritual maps.
Using 'gods' for angels can confuse believers trained to say there is only one God.

adherents: Michael S. Heiser and readers of *The Unseen Realm*
Many evangelical biblical scholars and teachers
Some Orthodox and Catholic scholars sympathetic to angelic hierarchies
Popular teaching such as the BibleProject's series on spiritual beings

positions.name: Evolutionary monotheism (from many gods to one by the exile)
positions.summary:
This view, held by most critical historians of religion, says Israel's belief in one God developed over several centuries. Early Israel emerged within Canaanite culture and shared much of its religion: the high god El, a council of divine 'sons', the storm god Baal, the goddess Asherah. Yahweh, perhaps originally a god from the southern regions of Edom and Midian ('Yahweh came from Teman', Hab 3:3), was increasingly identified with El and took over Baal's storm imagery. Over time Israel moved from many gods, to worship of Yahweh as the chief or only god for Israel (monolatry), to the claim that no other god exists.

Mark S. Smith describes two processes: 'convergence', in which Yahweh absorbed the titles and roles of El and some of Baal's, and 'differentiation', in which Israel rejected Baal, Asherah and child sacrifice as foreign. The decisive step to full monotheism came, on most accounts, in the late monarchy and especially the exile, when the loss of land, king and temple forced a choice: either Babylon's gods had won, or Yahweh was the only God and had used Babylon to judge his people. Isaiah 40–48 is read as the first clear expression of that conclusion.

positions.context: Julius Wellhausen's *Prolegomena* (1878) argued that strict monotheism and the priestly law were late, after the prophets. The discovery of the Ugaritic texts from 1929 and later Hebrew inscriptions (Khirbet el-Qom, published 1970; Kuntillet Ajrud, 1975–76) supplied direct evidence of the religious world around and within Israel. From the 1980s scholars such as Mark Smith, Albertz, Othmar Keel and Christoph Uehlinger combined texts, inscriptions and images into developmental histories. Within this broad consensus there is much disagreement about details and dates.
claims: Early Israelite religion grew out of, and shared much with, Canaanite religion.
Yahweh and El were originally distinct and later identified; Yahweh also took over Baal's storm-god imagery.
For much of the monarchy, many Israelites (including royal circles) worshipped Asherah, Baal and astral deities alongside Yahweh.
Biblical texts were shaped later by writers who projected a stricter faith back onto earlier periods.
Explicit monotheism, the denial that other gods exist, appears clearly only in the late monarchy and exile (Deut 4; Isa 40–48).

scriptures.reading: In its older form, Elyon divides the nations among the sons of God and Yahweh receives Israel, suggesting Yahweh was once one of El's sons.
A hymn to Yahweh as storm god, possibly adapted from a Canaanite Baal hymn; it calls on the 'sons of the mighty' (bene elim) to give him glory.
'God came from Teman' preserves a memory of Yahweh as a southern deity, matching 'Yahweh of Teman' at Kuntillet Ajrud.
The people say life was good when they burned incense to the Queen of Heaven, showing the goddess's deep roots in family religion.
An Asherah image stood in Yahweh's own temple, suggesting she was part of official worship for a time.
The first unmistakable denial that any other god exists, written in the exile.

arguments.text: Inscriptions from Kuntillet Ajrud (c. 800 BC) and Khirbet el-Qom bless people 'by Yahweh and his asherah', showing that Yahweh was associated with Asherah or her symbol in ordinary religion.

Ugaritic texts call El 'father of years', 'creator', and head of a council of his sons; Baal is the 'rider on the clouds'. Hebrew poetry uses the same titles of Yahweh (Ps 68:4; Dan 7:9), showing shared religious language.
The Bible itself admits that idolatry was the norm for most of the monarchy, including the royal court and temple (2 Kgs 21:3-7; 2 Kgs 23:4-14).

Exile explains the change: when a nation's god seems defeated, the people either abandon him or reinterpret history. Israel's prophets did the second, making Yahweh the Lord of all history (Isa 45:1-7).

critiques.text: Popular practice is not the same as normative faith. Showing that many Israelites worshipped Asherah does not show that Israel's covenant tradition approved of it, any more than medieval folk magic defines Christianity.
The developmental scheme depends on dating texts late and treating parallels as borrowing; read as a whole, the canon presents a coherent picture of one supreme God and created beings.
The theory can be circular: texts expressing monotheism are dated late because monotheism is assumed to be late.

responses.text: Developmental historians agree on the distinction and use it (Albertz's 'official' and 'family' religion). The point is that the evidence for the official cult itself, such as an Asherah in the temple, shows that the line between orthodox and popular moved over time.
The canon is coherent because later editors shaped it; historians ask what happened before that shaping. Both readings can be valid, but they answer different questions.
Dates rest on many independent factors (language, historical references, inscriptions), not only on theology. Even some conservative scholars accept that Isa 40–55 addresses the exile.

strawMen.strawMan: Evolutionary scholars think the Bible is just borrowed pagan myth.
strawMen.correction: Most stress how Israel transformed what it inherited, and many are religious believers who see development as part of how revelation happened.

strawMen.strawMan: They claim Israel worshipped Baal officially from the start.
strawMen.correction: Most say Baal worship was always contested; the claim is that Yahweh's own early profile overlapped with El and Baal, not that Baal was Israel's official god.

positive: Takes archaeology and Near Eastern texts seriously and explains why the prophets fought so hard.
Shows the exile as a theological turning point and helps readers see why Isaiah 40–55 sounds so new.
negative: Can make the biblical story of covenant and apostasy look like later propaganda.
Can be unsettling for believers if presented as if it settled theological questions it does not address.

positions.name: The 'Yahweh-alone' movement (a minority that won)
positions.summary:
This view agrees with evolutionary accounts that most Israelites for most of their history worshipped several gods. But it explains the change differently: not as a slow, natural evolution, but as a long struggle between a determined minority and the majority. A 'Yahweh-alone' party, beginning with prophets like Elijah and Hosea in the northern kingdom, insisted that Israel must worship Yahweh only. It was persecuted, gained influence under Hezekiah, lost it under Manasseh, gained power again with Josiah's reform (2 Kgs 23) and was vindicated, in its own eyes, by the exile.

Because this group's followers collected, edited and preserved most of the Hebrew Bible, the story is told from the winners' side. The kings who tolerated other gods are judged evil; the reformers are judged good. Morton Smith first argued for 'parties' shaping the Old Testament; Bernhard Lang developed the idea of a 'prophetic minority' whose demand for monolatry (worship of one God) became full monotheism after 586 BC. The view takes the Bible's own picture of a faithful remnant very seriously, but reads that remnant as the origin of exclusive Yahweh worship rather than its preserver.

positions.context: The idea grew out of the sociological study of religion in the 1960s and 1970s, which looked at groups, interests and power. It explains why the Hebrew Bible is so polemical: it was written in the middle of a fight. It shares the evidence of evolutionary views (Ugarit, inscriptions, figurines) but stresses conflict and human agents over gradual change. It also takes the biblical remnant motif (1 Kgs 19:18) seriously as history, which gives it an unexpected point of contact with traditional readings.
claims: Most Israelites, including kings and priests, were polytheists or worshipped Yahweh alongside other gods for most of the monarchy.
A minority movement demanded worship of Yahweh alone, starting in the ninth century with prophets such as Elijah and later Hosea.
The movement's fortunes rose and fell with royal politics: Hezekiah, then Manasseh, then Josiah.
Its followers edited the historical books and prophets, so the Bible tells the story from its point of view.
Monolatry became monotheism after the exile, when the movement's warnings seemed fulfilled.

scriptures.reading: Elijah's either-or demand defines the movement: Yahweh or Baal, not both.
Seven thousand who have not bowed to Baal: a small faithful minority.
Israel must no longer call Yahweh 'my Baal'; the names of the Baals will be removed.
Hezekiah removes high places and even Nehushtan, an early reform victory.
Manasseh reverses everything: the majority religion returns with royal backing.
Josiah's reform: the movement gains state power and enforces its programme.

arguments.text: The biblical narrative itself describes a small group of faithful prophets and reformers against kings, priests and most of the people (1 Kgs 19:10; Jer 44:15-18).
The reforms of Hezekiah and Josiah, and the reversal under Manasseh, fit a pattern of factional struggle better than a smooth evolution.

The Elephantine papyri (5th century BC) show a Jewish colony in Egypt honouring Yahu alongside Anat-Yahu and other names, showing that wider Yahwism survived where the reformers' influence did not reach.
The strongly polemical tone of Deuteronomy and Kings, and their judgement of kings by a single test (worship at Jerusalem, no other gods), point to authors with a programme.

critiques.text: Talk of a single 'party' with a stable programme across three centuries goes beyond the evidence and may project modern political categories onto ancient religious life.
The movement always claimed to be calling Israel back to the covenant of Moses. The theory assumes that claim was false rather than showing it.
The view tends to treat all 'gods' language as leftover polytheism, missing that even the strictest prophets speak of a heavenly host serving Yahweh (Isa 6:1-8).

responses.text: Defenders such as Lang describe a loose movement or tradition, not a formal party; the label is shorthand for a recurring prophetic and reforming stream.
Historians cannot simply accept the claims of one side in a dispute. The question is whether there is evidence of exclusive Yahwism before the ninth century, and that evidence is thin and contested.
A subordinate heavenly host is compatible with monolatry. The theory concerns worship, not cosmology, and agrees that council imagery survived the reform.

strawMen.strawMan: The theory says the prophets made everything up for power.
strawMen.correction: Most defenders see the movement as sincere and religiously serious; the point is that it was a minority, not that it was cynical.

strawMen.strawMan: It denies any connection between Moses and later faith.
strawMen.correction: Some versions allow early roots of exclusive Yahweh devotion; the claim is that it became dominant only late.

positive: Explains the intensely polemical character of the historical books and prophets.
Highlights the courage of prophetic minorities, a theme that resonates with the Bible's own remnant theology.
negative: Can reduce theology to group politics.
Can encourage reading the biblical narrative with suspicion everywhere, making it hard to hear its claims on their own terms.

readings.reading: Many classical readers follow the traditional Hebrew text, 'according to the number of the sons of Israel', and see God arranging the nations with Israel at the centre. Those who accept the Qumran reading 'sons of God' usually take them as angels serving God, not as gods with real independence.

The Qumran and Greek reading 'sons of God' is original. After Babel, the Most High gave the nations to lesser divine beings and kept Israel as his own portion. This explains why the nations worship other gods and why the New Testament speaks of rulers and authorities over them.

An old poetic fragment in which 'the Most High' (Elyon, originally El, the high god) divides the nations among his sons, and Yahweh is one of those sons receiving Israel. Later scribes found this embarrassing and changed 'sons of God' to 'sons of Israel'.

A survival of the older, wider religion that the Yahweh-alone party absorbed into its own literature. The later scribal change to 'sons of Israel' shows the party tidying up its inheritance as its theology hardened.
The 'gods' are human rulers and judges acting with God's delegated authority, as in older Jewish and Christian readings; or, at most, angels. The psalm is about justice, not a pantheon.

God presides over a real assembly of divine beings and condemns them for misruling the nations. They are created and will 'die like men' (Ps 82:7). Yahweh is the God of gods, not one god among equals.

A snapshot of the change in progress. The old council of El is still pictured, but Israel's God now stands up within it and sentences the other gods to death, leaving himself as the only real deity over all nations.
Polemic from the Yahweh-alone side: the gods of the popular religion are put on trial and declared mortal. The psalm dramatises the party's claim that all other cults are doomed.
'The LORD our God, the LORD is one' affirms that there is only one true God and that Israel owes him undivided love. It is the root of later Jewish and Christian monotheism.
The Shema stresses Yahweh's uniqueness and Israel's exclusive loyalty ('the LORD alone'). It does not deny that other spiritual beings exist; it denies that any of them is in Yahweh's class.

Originally a call to exclusive worship (monolatry), possibly also a rejection of local versions of Yahweh such as 'Yahweh of Samaria' and 'Yahweh of Teman'. It was later read as a statement that only one God exists.
The party's watchword: Israel must serve Yahweh alone. Its demand for undivided loyalty is the programme of the Deuteronomic reformers under Josiah.
'I am the LORD, and there is none else; there is no God beside me' says plainly what Israel always meant: only Yahweh is God. Isaiah is spelling out an old faith against Babylonian idolatry.

An incomparability claim. Babylon and Nineveh use the same phrase about themselves (Isa 47:8; Zeph 2:15) without meaning that no other city exists. Yahweh has no rival, but created spirits still exist.
The first clear statements of full monotheism, written in the exile around 540 BC. Here other gods are no longer rivals or subordinates; they are nothing.
The theological victory of the party, stated with new sharpness when the exile seemed to vindicate its warnings and Babylon's gods proved powerless.
'Who is like unto thee, O LORD, among the gods?' is a poetic way of saying the gods of Egypt proved to be nothing beside the true God. It does not grant them real existence.
An early song comparing Yahweh with real spiritual powers he has just defeated in judging Egypt's gods (Exod 12:12; Num 33:4). He is incomparable among the elohim.
Very old poetry that assumes many gods exist and praises Yahweh as the strongest. This is monolatry, not monotheism.
Shows the early, warrior form of Yahweh devotion that the party later built on: a jealous God who outclasses the gods of the nations.
Elijah calls Israel back to the faith it already knew: 'If the LORD be God, follow him: but if Baal, then follow him.' The contest exposes Baal as no god at all (1 Kgs 18:39).
A showdown between Yahweh and a foreign deity's cult on Baal's own ground (fire and rain). Baal is powerless; whatever spiritual power stands behind him cannot answer.
Evidence that in the ninth century many Israelites saw nothing wrong in worshipping Yahweh and Baal together. Elijah's either-or is a newer, stricter demand.
Elijah is the movement's hero and founder figure. The story shows a minority prophet against a royal, syncretistic establishment.

Josiah removes Baal, Asherah and the host of heaven from the temple, proving that these were intrusions into Israel's true faith. Inscriptions such as Kuntillet Ajrud ('Yahweh of Samaria and his asherah', c. 800 BC) show the popular apostasy the prophets condemned, not the official faith.

The reform purges the worship of the host of heaven and other powers. Kuntillet Ajrud shows how ordinary Israelites blurred Yahweh with other beings; the biblical writers treat that as rebellion, not as Israel's norm.

The reform removes things that had long been normal parts of Jerusalem religion, including an asherah in Yahweh's own temple. Kuntillet Ajrud and Khirbet el-Qom suggest that many Israelites honoured Asherah (or her symbol) alongside Yahweh.
The decisive moment when the minority party gained royal power and enforced its programme. What it removed had been the religion of the majority.

The first commandment and the Shema demand exclusive worship from Sinai onward.
Deuteronomy already says there is none besides Yahweh in heaven or on earth.
Inscriptions like Kuntillet Ajrud and the prophets' own complaints show many Israelites, including kings, worshipped other gods.
The Bible itself says this: it presents the official faith and the popular practice as being at war.
Yahweh was always unique, but the Bible affirms other created divine beings (elohim) in his council.
Texts plainly speak of the council and the sons of God.
Paul calls idols nothing yet says sacrifices go to demons, so both claims can stand together.
Calling created spirits 'gods' blurs the line the prophets drew; Isaiah says other gods are nothing.
The same 'none besides me' formula is used by Babylon and Nineveh of themselves; it means 'without rival', not 'alone in existence'.
Israel's religion grew from Canaanite roots into monotheism by the exile.
Yahweh shares El's titles and Baal's storm imagery, as Ugaritic parallels show.
Shared language does not prove shared belief; borrowed images can be used polemically against the gods they came from.
Polemic explains some passages but not the sheer amount of everyday evidence: figurines, inscriptions and royal shrines.
A minority Yahweh-alone party fought a polytheistic majority and wrote the story after it won.
The prophets repeatedly present themselves as a small faithful remnant against kings and people.
A 'party' with a coherent platform is hard to show from the evidence; the model may read modern politics into ancient religion.
The minority claimed to be calling Israel back to an older covenant, which the theory assumes rather than disproves was false.

title: Who are the 'gods' judged in Psalm 82?
question: In Psalm 82 God stands 'in the congregation of the mighty' and judges 'among the gods', then says 'I have said, Ye are gods… but ye shall die like men.' Are these gods heavenly beings, human judges, or Israel itself? And what did Jesus mean when he quoted the psalm in John 10?
intro:
Psalm 82 is only eight verses long, but it is one of the most argued-over passages in the Old Testament. God takes his place in a gathering called the 'congregation of God' (adat-el) and judges in the middle of the elohim, a Hebrew word that usually means 'God' or 'gods' but can occasionally refer to other powerful figures. He accuses them of judging unjustly and favouring the wicked, demands justice for the poor and fatherless, then pronounces: 'I have said, Ye are gods; and all of you are children of the most High. But ye shall die like men, and fall like one of the princes.' The psalm ends with a prayer: 'Arise, O God, judge the earth: for thou shalt inherit all nations.'

Three readings have a long history. Many modern scholars, and the divine-council view popular among evangelicals, read the 'gods' as heavenly beings who were meant to govern the nations and failed. A long Jewish and Christian tradition reads them as human rulers and judges, who exercise God's authority and can be called 'gods' because of their office. A rabbinic reading links the verse to Israel at Mount Sinai: when Israel received the Torah it was like the immortal angels, but by sinning with the golden calf it fell back into mortality.

The question matters partly because Jesus quotes Ps 82:6 when accused of blasphemy (John 10:34-36). How his argument works depends on whom the psalm addressed.

positions.name: Heavenly beings of the divine council
positions.summary:
On this reading, Psalm 82 pictures a heavenly courtroom. God (Elohim, here standing for Yahweh) rises in the 'assembly of El' and passes sentence on the other elohim, divine beings to whom he had given responsibility for the nations. They have ruled unjustly, letting the poor be crushed, and so they will lose their immortality and 'die like men'. The psalm ends with a prayer that God himself will take over the nations they misgoverned.

This is the majority view in modern critical scholarship, from Hermann Gunkel and Hans-Joachim Kraus to many recent commentators, and it is central to the evangelical divine-council theology popularised by Michael Heiser. Defenders note the close parallels with the council of El in the Ugaritic texts, with Ps 89:5-7 and with Deut 32:8-9 in its Qumran form. They also note that it was already a Jewish reading before Christ: the Qumran Melchizedek scroll pictures a heavenly figure judging among the elohim using Ps 82:1. Christian defenders read the psalm as part of a biblical story in which rebellious powers are disarmed by Christ and the nations are reclaimed (Col 2:15; Rev 11:15).

figures.bio: Made Ps 82 the entry point of a whole-Bible theology of the divine council, arguing that it explains Deut 32, the 'principalities and powers' and the mission to the nations.

positions.context: Interest in this reading grew after the Ugaritic tablets (discovered from 1929) revealed a council of El with 'sons of El' that closely resembles biblical language. But the reading is older than modern scholarship: Second Temple Jews at Qumran used Ps 82:1 of heavenly judgement, and some early Christian writers understood the gods as heavenly powers. Today it is the default among critical scholars and widely held among evangelicals influenced by Heiser and the BibleProject.
claims: Adat-el ('assembly of El/God') is a technical term for the heavenly council, matching Ugaritic usage.
The 'gods' are created spiritual beings given authority over the nations (Deut 32:8-9).
They are condemned for corrupt rule and sentenced to lose their immortality.
Ps 82:8 anticipates God reclaiming the nations from these powers.
Jesus' use of Ps 82 in John 10 shows that 'god' and 'son of the Most High' language for beings other than Yahweh is scriptural, so his claim is not blasphemy in principle.

scriptures.reading: God stands in the assembly of El and judges among the gods.
The punishment, to 'die like men', only makes sense for beings who were not mortal.
A parallel council of holy ones in the heavens, among whom Yahweh is incomparable.
The nations were allotted to the sons of God; Ps 82:8 reverses that allotment.
Another heavenly court scene with the host of heaven standing around God's throne.
Christ disarms rulers and authorities, which Christian defenders link to the fall of the gods in Ps 82.

arguments.text: The parallel between 'gods' and 'sons of the Most High' (Ps 82:6) matches the use of 'sons of God' for heavenly beings in Job and Ps 89.
The contrast 'you are gods… but you shall die like men' is powerful only if the hearers are not men. Human judges dying 'like men' would be no sentence at all.
The Qumran Melchizedek scroll (11Q13) quotes Ps 82:1 of a heavenly judge among divine beings, showing the reading existed among Jews before Christ.
Ugaritic texts describe the 'assembly of El' and the 'sons of El' in nearly the same words, giving a known background for the scene.

critiques.text: The accusations (partiality, failing the fatherless and poor) are precisely the duties of Israel's human judges, so the psalm reads naturally as a rebuke of corrupt courts.
Jesus says the 'gods' were those to whom 'the word of God came'. That describes humans who received revelation, not angels.
Calling created beings 'gods' who are judged and die risks a quasi-polytheistic picture that later biblical writers rejected.

responses.text: Ancient people saw heavenly powers as the guardians of justice in their nations (cf. Dan 10:13, 20). Injustice on earth is the failure of rulers in heaven and on earth together.
The 'word of God' in John 10:35 may be the word of judgement spoken to them in the psalm itself ('I said, you are gods'). Jesus' point is that Scripture uses such language and cannot be broken.
The psalm itself denies the gods any independence: they are appointed, judged and sentenced by the one God. That is a strong statement of God's sole sovereignty, not a concession to polytheism.

strawMen.strawMan: This view says the Bible accepts pagan gods as real deities equal to Yahweh.
strawMen.correction: It says the reverse: God judges all such beings as his subordinates and strips them of their status.

strawMen.strawMan: This is a recent internet theory.
strawMen.correction: It is the mainstream view of modern Psalms commentaries and has ancient Jewish precedents at Qumran.

positive: Explains the strong mythic language of the psalm without strain.
Links the Old Testament to New Testament teaching on spiritual powers and Christ's victory over them.
negative: Can encourage speculation about named territorial spirits.
Makes John 10 harder to explain for some readers.

positions.name: Human judges and rulers
positions.summary:
This reading takes the 'gods' to be human judges, kings and magistrates. In Israel judges acted for God: bringing a case before them was bringing it 'before God' (Exod 22:8-9, where the KJV and older Jewish tradition translate elohim as 'the judges'). Because they carried God's authority, they could be called 'gods' and 'children of the most High', just as Moses was made 'a god to Pharaoh' (Exod 7:1). Psalm 82 is a prophetic rebuke: God stands among Israel's rulers, condemns their corrupt justice, and reminds them that for all their title they are mortal and will fall.

The view has deep roots in Jewish interpretation (the Aramaic Targum renders the scene in terms of judges, and Rashi follows it) and became standard in Christian commentary from the Reformation onward, through Calvin, Matthew Henry and Spurgeon. Its defenders stress the psalm's ethical content, which concerns orphans, the poor and bribery, and they read Jesus' quotation in John 10 as a straightforward lesser-to-greater argument: if Scripture calls human judges 'gods' because God's word appointed them, how much more can the one sent by the Father call himself God's Son.

figures.name: Rashi (Rabbi Shlomo Yitzchaki)
figures.bio: The most influential Jewish commentator on the Bible and Talmud. His Psalms commentary reads the 'gods' as judges, consistent with the Targum and with rabbinic use of elohim for courts.

works.title: Commentary on Psalms

figures.name: John Calvin
figures.bio: Read Ps 82 as addressed to rulers and magistrates, whose authority is a gift from God that makes their injustice more culpable. His reading shaped Reformed political thought about rulers as God's servants.

works.title: Commentary on the Book of Psalms

figures.name: Charles H. Spurgeon
figures.bio: His seven-volume devotional commentary on the Psalms presented the 'gods' as magistrates and judges and applied the psalm to rulers of his own day.

positions.context: Jewish interpreters had reason to avoid reading the psalm as a scene among many gods, and the Targum's 'judges' reading became standard in rabbinic commentary. In Christianity, the Reformers' focus on civil authority and on plain, ethical sense made the magistrates reading natural. It dominated English-language commentary until the twentieth century and is still held by many pastors and some scholars, especially because of how it explains John 10.
claims: Elohim can refer to human judges as God's representatives (Exod 21:6; Exod 22:8-9 in traditional translation).
Rulers are 'gods' by office and commission, not by nature (Exod 7:1).
The psalm condemns real courts that favour the wicked and ignore the poor.
'You shall die like men' warns that office does not exempt rulers from mortality and judgement.
In John 10, Jesus argues from human judges who bore God's word to himself as the one the Father sanctified and sent.

scriptures.reading: Cases are brought to 'the judges' (elohim), who decide in God's name.
Moses is made 'a god to Pharaoh': human beings can carry the title by appointment.
Judges must not show partiality, 'for the judgment is God's'.
Jehoshaphat tells his judges they judge 'not for man, but for the LORD'.
The charges are judicial: unjust verdicts and neglect of the poor and fatherless.
A lesser-to-greater argument from human 'gods' to the Son of God.

arguments.text: The duties in Ps 82:3-4 are almost word for word the commands to Israel's human judges in the law.
In 2 Chr 19:6-7, judges are told that they judge for the LORD, which explains how they can represent him and be called by his title.
Jesus' argument in John 10 is clearest if the 'gods' are humans: if humans who received God's word are called gods, how much less is it blasphemy for the Son to say he is God's Son.
The Aramaic Targum and later rabbinic commentary read the scene in terms of judges, showing a long Jewish tradition behind this interpretation.

critiques.text: The sentence 'you shall die like men' would be meaningless if the judges were already men; the contrast requires non-human hearers.
Most scholars now think elohim in Exod 21:6 and 22:8-9 means 'God' (at the sanctuary), not 'judges', which removes the main evidence that judges were called elohim.
The rabbis who connected the psalm to Sinai read it as about the whole people, not a class of officials; restricting it to judges narrows Jesus' 'to whom the word of God came'.

responses.text: The contrast is between their exalted title and their mortal fate: they act as 'gods' but will die like any common man and fall like other princes. That is a real and humbling sentence.
Even if Exod 22 means 'before God', the point stands that judges act for God; and Moses as 'god' to Pharaoh shows the title can be used by delegation.
The two readings can combine: Israel's rulers were the leading recipients of God's word, and Jesus' argument works either way.

strawMen.strawMan: This view is just an embarrassed modern attempt to avoid the supernatural.
strawMen.correction: It is many centuries older than modern scepticism, rooted in the Targum, Rashi and the Reformers, who all believed in angels.

strawMen.strawMan: It says rulers are divine.
strawMen.correction: It says rulers are called 'gods' only because they represent God, and the psalm exists to humble them.

positive: Grounds a strong biblical ethic of just government accountable to God.
Gives a simple reading of Jesus' argument in John 10.
negative: Can flatten the psalm's mythic and cosmic setting.
Can be used to exalt rulers' authority if its warnings are ignored.

John Calvin and much Reformed commentary
Matthew Henry and Charles Spurgeon
Many modern pastors and some evangelical scholars

positions.name: Israel at Sinai
positions.summary:
A third reading, found in rabbinic literature, connects Psalm 82 with Israel's experience at Mount Sinai. When Israel received the Torah and said 'we will do, and be obedient' (Exod 24:7), God declared them 'gods' and 'children of the most High': in the rabbinic telling, they were freed from the power of death and became like the angels. But when they made the golden calf (Exod 32), they lost that status, and God said, 'you shall die like men', that is, like Adam, who also lost life through disobedience. The Babylonian Talmud (Avodah Zarah 5a) gives this interpretation, and later midrash develops it.

Some New Testament scholars, especially Jerome Neyrey, argue that this reading explains John 10:34-36 best. Jesus defines the 'gods' as 'them to whom the word of God came', which fits Israel receiving God's word at Sinai. His argument is then: if Israel was called 'gods' because it received the word, how much more the one who is himself the Word (John 1:1, 14), consecrated and sent by the Father. Early Christian writers such as Irenaeus developed a related idea, applying 'you are gods' to all who receive adoption through the Word, which became part of the Eastern Christian teaching on deification (theosis).

positions.context: The rabbinic tradition read Scripture as a connected whole and often linked psalms to events in the Torah. The connection between Sinai and immortality also appears in other midrashic traditions about the tablets being 'engraved' (harut, read as herut, freedom from the angel of death) in Exod 32:16. In Christian scholarship the reading became prominent mainly through studies of John's Gospel, where commentators noticed how well it fits Jesus' phrase about the word of God coming to people.
claims: The 'congregation of God' is Israel, gathered to receive the Torah.
'I said, you are gods' refers to God's declaration over Israel at Sinai.
'You shall die like men' refers to the loss of that status after the golden calf.
Jesus' phrase 'to whom the word of God came' points directly to Israel receiving the Torah.
Jesus' lesser-to-greater argument contrasts those who received the Word with the Word himself.

scriptures.reading: At Sinai Israel is called God's treasured possession and a kingdom of priests.
Israel promises, 'All that the LORD hath said will we do, and be obedient.'
The golden calf: the fall that rabbinic tradition links with 'you shall die like men'.
Israel is God's firstborn son, matching 'children of the most High'.
'Them to whom the word of God came' describes those who received revelation.
Jesus is the Word made flesh, greater than those to whom the word merely came.

arguments.text: John 10:35 defines the 'gods' as those to whom God's word came. That fits Israel at Sinai more naturally than heavenly beings or a select group of judges.
Israel is called God's son (Exod 4:22; Deut 14:1; Hos 11:1), so 'sons of the Most High' is natural language for the nation.
The Talmud and midrash show this was a known Jewish interpretation, and Neyrey argues traces of it can be detected in the first century.
The pattern of gift (life through the word), sin (the calf) and death (dying like Adam) echoes Gen 2–3, a frequent rabbinic and biblical pattern.

critiques.text: Nothing in Psalm 82 mentions Sinai, Torah or the calf. The link depends on later rabbinic exegesis, whose first-century existence is uncertain.
The psalm's charges concern judicial corruption, which fits officials better than the whole nation.
The rabbinic sources are written down centuries after John; using them to explain John risks anachronism.

responses.text: Psalms often allude to Israel's story without naming it. And whatever the psalm's original sense, John's wording suggests that a Sinai-related reading was known to Jesus' hearers.
Israel as a whole was told to do justice (Deut 16:20), and the psalm's charge can apply to the nation and its leaders together.
Defenders admit the dating problem but note that rabbinic traditions often preserve older material, and the fit with John's exact words is itself evidence.

strawMen.strawMan: This view says Israel was literally divine.
strawMen.correction: It says Israel received a gift of life and closeness to God that it lost by sin; 'gods' describes privilege, not nature.

strawMen.strawMan: It is a purely Jewish reading Christians cannot use.
strawMen.correction: Christian scholars such as Neyrey defend it for John 10, and it resonates with patristic teaching on adoption and deification.

positive: Gives a close fit for Jesus' words in John 10.
Connects the psalm to the great biblical pattern of gift, fall and restoration.
negative: Depends on traditions recorded later than the New Testament.
Can obscure the psalm's original concern for social justice.

Jerome Neyrey and some Johannine scholars
Some patristic and Eastern Orthodox readings linked to deification
Some Jewish commentators who combine it with the judges reading

readings.reading: 'Congregation of the mighty' is literally 'the assembly of El', the same phrase used at Ugarit for the council of the gods. God stands up to judge the members of his own heavenly council.
God stands in the 'congregation' of Israel (adat is regularly Israel's assembly, e.g. Num 27:17) and judges the judges who sit in it. The ancient Targum and Rashi read it this way.
The assembly is Israel itself, gathered as God's congregation. The 'gods' are the people who stood at Sinai and were given the Torah.
The heavenly rulers of the nations have allowed injustice to flourish on earth; the nations' oppression reflects the failure of their spiritual overseers.
This is plain judicial language: showing partiality, failing to defend the poor and fatherless. These are the duties Israel's law gives human judges (Deut 1:16-17; Deut 16:18-20).
Israel, having received God's law, was meant to be a just people; the charge is that the nation and its leaders failed to live out the Torah they received.
'Children of the most High' (bene elyon) parallels 'sons of God', a phrase that elsewhere means heavenly beings (Job 1:6; Job 38:7). God appointed them and gave them their status.
'I said' recalls God's appointment of judges as his representatives; they are 'gods' by office, as Moses was made 'a god to Pharaoh' (Exod 7:1).
'I said, you are gods' refers to the moment at Sinai when Israel accepted the Torah and, in rabbinic tradition, was freed from the angel of death.
The shock is that immortal beings are sentenced to die 'like men' (like Adam). Their punishment is the loss of their immortality and rule.
Despite their high office, these judges are mortal and will fall like any prince. Power does not exempt them from God's judgement.
After the golden calf (Exod 32), Israel lost the immortality it had been given at Sinai and became mortal 'like Adam'.
With the failed gods removed, God himself will take possession of all the nations once allotted to them (Deut 32:8-9). Christians see this fulfilled in Christ's mission to the nations.
Where human justice has failed, the psalmist asks God to judge the earth directly, for all nations belong to him.
The God of Sinai is not only Israel's God; the psalm closes by looking to his rule over every nation.
Elohim here means God himself: the case is brought 'before God' at the sanctuary. It does not prove that human judges were called gods.
The KJV, following older Jewish tradition, translates elohim as 'the judges'. This shows that the word could refer to human judges acting for God.
Shows that God's authority is shared with Israel's own institutions; the people who received the law also exercise it.

Jesus argues that Scripture itself calls beings other than Yahweh 'gods' and 'sons of the Most High', so his claim to be God's Son cannot be ruled blasphemous in principle. As the one the Father sanctified and sent, he is far greater than they. Defenders admit 'to whom the word of God came' is the hardest phrase for this view; they read it as those addressed by God's word of judgement in the psalm.

A lesser-to-greater argument: if Scripture calls mere human judges 'gods' because God's word commissioned them, how much more may the one whom the Father consecrated and sent into the world be called Son of God.

'Those to whom the word of God came' are Israel at Sinai, who received the Torah. If receiving God's word made them 'gods', how much more the one who is himself the Word (John 1:1, 14), sanctified and sent by the Father.

title: Who were the sons of God and the Nephilim?
question: In Genesis 6:1-4 'the sons of God saw the daughters of men' and took wives, and 'there were giants (Nephilim) in the earth in those days'. Were the sons of God fallen angels, the godly descendants of Seth, or ancient kings? And who were the Nephilim?
intro:
Just before the flood, Genesis tells a four-verse story that has puzzled readers for over two thousand years. 'The sons of God saw the daughters of men that they were fair; and they took them wives of all which they chose' (Gen 6:2). God limits human life to 120 years. Then: 'There were giants (Hebrew Nephilim) in the earth in those days; and also after that, when the sons of God came in unto the daughters of men, and they bare children to them, the same became mighty men which were of old, men of renown' (Gen 6:4). Immediately afterwards God sees that human wickedness is great and resolves to send the flood.

Three main readings exist, and each arose at a different time. The oldest known interpretation, in the Jewish Book of the Watchers (1 Enoch, third century BC), says the sons of God were angels who left heaven, married women and fathered giants; Jude and 2 Peter seem to echo this, and most early Church Fathers held it. From the second century AD, rabbis rejected the angel reading and took the sons of God as sons of nobles or judges, a view developed by modern scholars as 'royal tyrants' who claimed divine sonship. From the third century, Christian writers such as Julius Africanus, and decisively Augustine, read the sons of God as the godly line of Seth marrying ungodly Cainite women, which became standard in the medieval church and among many Reformers.

The Nephilim appear once more, in the spies' report that they saw 'the giants, the sons of Anak, which come of the giants' in Canaan (Num 13:33). How that verse relates to Gen 6 is part of the debate.

positions.name: Fallen angels (the Watchers)
positions.summary:
On this view the 'sons of God' were heavenly beings who crossed the boundary God had set between heaven and earth. They took human wives, and their children were the Nephilim, the famous 'mighty men' of ancient legend. The episode shows corruption spreading beyond humanity into the created order itself, and it is the immediate background to the flood. The phrase 'sons of God' is used elsewhere in the Hebrew Bible for heavenly beings (Job 1:6; Job 2:1; Job 38:7), and the New Testament letters of Jude and 2 Peter speak of angels who 'left their own habitation', committed a sin compared with Sodom's, and are kept in chains until the judgement.

This is the oldest interpretation on record. The Book of the Watchers (1 Enoch 6–16, third century BC) tells of 200 'Watchers' led by Shemihazah who swore an oath on Mount Hermon, married women, taught forbidden arts such as sorcery and metalworking for war, and fathered giants whose violence filled the earth. Jubilees, Josephus and the Septuagint tradition (some manuscripts read 'angels of God' in Gen 6:2) reflect the same understanding, as do most Christian writers of the second and third centuries. In 1 Enoch the spirits of the dead giants become evil spirits, an idea some modern defenders use to explain the origin of demons, though Scripture itself does not say this. Many modern critical scholars and a growing number of evangelicals hold this reading.

positions.context: The view dominated Jewish interpretation in the Second Temple period and Christian interpretation until the fourth century. It fell out of favour when rabbis in the second century and Christian writers from the third century rejected the idea of angels marrying. It returned in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries with critical scholarship (which saw a myth fragment in the passage) and with evangelical scholars who argued from the usage of 'sons of God' and from Jude and 2 Peter. Michael Heiser's *Reversing Hermon* (2017) made it popular again.
claims: 'Sons of God' in the Hebrew Bible means heavenly beings.
These beings transgressed God's boundaries by taking human wives.
Their offspring were the Nephilim, mighty warriors remembered in legend.
Jude and 2 Peter confirm an angelic sin in the days of Noah, followed by imprisonment.
The episode explains why the corruption before the flood was so extreme.

scriptures.reading: The 'sons of God' come to present themselves before the LORD in heaven.
The 'sons of God' shout for joy at creation, before humans existed.
The Nephilim and mighty men appear when the sons of God go in to the daughters of men.
Angels who left their dwelling are compared with Sodom going after 'strange flesh'.
Sinning angels cast into Tartarus are mentioned alongside the flood.
Christ proclaims to 'spirits in prison' who disobeyed in the days of Noah, which many link to the same angels.

arguments.text: Every other use of the exact Hebrew phrase bene ha-elohim refers to heavenly beings, so the burden of proof is on readings that make them human.
Jude ties the angels' sin to sexual transgression ('in like manner… strange flesh') and quotes 1 Enoch, showing the apostolic writers knew and used the Watcher tradition.
The angelic reading is the earliest interpretation we have, attested in 1 Enoch, Jubilees, Josephus and nearly all early Christian writers before the third century.
The contrast 'sons of God' and 'daughters of men' naturally sets a divine category against a human one, and the extraordinary offspring suggest an extraordinary union.

critiques.text: Jesus says angels do not marry (Matt 22:30), and spiritual beings cannot father physical children.
God's judgement in Gen 6:3 and 6:5-7 is on humanity, which makes more sense if humans were the main offenders.
Jude and 2 Peter may be using a well-known tradition as an illustration without endorsing it as the meaning of Genesis.

responses.text: Jesus speaks of angels 'in heaven', in their proper state; Jude speaks of angels who abandoned that state. Angels in Genesis eat and are taken for men (Gen 18:1-8; Gen 19:1-5), so the Bible does not treat them as unable to take bodily form.
Humans took part willingly, and the corruption spread to 'all flesh' (Gen 6:12). The angels are judged separately (2 Pet 2:4).
Jude cites 1 Enoch as prophecy (Jude 1:14) and assumes his readers share the tradition; both letters place the angelic sin in sequence with the flood.

strawMen.correction: It is the oldest Jewish and Christian interpretation and is held by many respected scholars today.

strawMen.correction: Defenders distinguish what Genesis, Jude and Peter say from the details 1 Enoch adds, such as names, numbers and Mount Hermon.

Explains the scale of the corruption before the flood and links to biblical themes of rebellious powers.
negative: Can feed speculation about modern 'hybrids', giants and conspiracy theories.
Can make humans look like passive victims rather than responsible sinners.

positions.name: The godly line of Seth
positions.summary:
This view reads Genesis 6 in the light of chapters 4 and 5, which trace two family lines. The line of Cain builds cities, develops crafts and produces the violent, boastful Lamech (Gen 4:17-24). The line of Seth begins to 'call upon the name of the LORD' (Gen 4:26) and includes Enoch, who 'walked with God' (Gen 5:24). The 'sons of God' are the descendants of Seth, God's people; the 'daughters of men' are women of the godless line. When the godly chose wives only for beauty, the distinction between the two lines dissolved, faith collapsed, and the world became so corrupt that only Noah's family was left.

The reading first appears clearly in the Christian chronographer Julius Africanus (early third century), was developed by Syriac writers such as Ephrem, given classic form by Augustine (*City of God* 15.23) and John Chrysostom, and became the standard view of the medieval church and of Reformers including Luther and Calvin. Its defenders argue that it keeps the story about human sin and human judgement, takes Jesus' words about angels not marrying seriously, and reflects a theme that runs through the whole Bible: the danger of God's people being absorbed by unbelief through marriage (Deut 7:3-4; Neh 13:23-27; 2 Cor 6:14).

positions.context: By the third century, Christian theologians increasingly saw angels as purely spiritual beings, and the angels-marrying story seemed both impossible and in conflict with Matt 22:30. The Sethite reading offered a moral, human interpretation that fitted the genealogies of Genesis. After Augustine it dominated Western Christianity for more than a thousand years and remained common among Protestant commentators such as Keil and Delitzsch. It is still held widely in conservative churches.
claims: Gen 4–5 sets up two lines: the ungodly line of Cain and the godly line of Seth.
The 'sons of God' are Seth's descendants, God's people; the 'daughters of men' are from the ungodly line.
The sin was intermarriage that dissolved the boundary between belief and unbelief.
Angels do not marry or reproduce (Matt 22:30), so the sons of God must be human.
The Nephilim were violent strong men, not hybrid beings.

scriptures.reading: In Seth's days people began to call on the name of the LORD, marking a godly line.
Enoch of Seth's line walked with God, showing what the godly line was meant to be.
Lamech of Cain's line, with two wives and a boast of revenge, shows the ungodly line's character.
'Ye are the children of the LORD your God': God's people can be called his sons.
Angels do not marry, so they cannot be the husbands in Gen 6.
Marriage with unbelievers turns hearts away from God, the sin the Sethite reading sees in Gen 6.

arguments.text: The literary context is the two genealogies of Gen 4 and Gen 5, which are deliberately contrasted. Gen 6:1-4 naturally continues that story.
The judgement that follows targets humans: God's spirit will not strive with 'man', and 'man's' wickedness is great.
Angels are spirits (Heb 1:14) and do not marry; a union producing children is outside their nature as Scripture describes it.
The view became the consensus of the Western church from Augustine through the Reformation, reflecting careful theological reflection on angels.

critiques.text: 'Sons of God' never means the line of Seth anywhere else, and the exact phrase elsewhere means heavenly beings.
In Gen 6:1 'daughters' are born to humanity in general. Making 'daughters of men' mean only Cainite women in the next verse is an unsignalled change.
Why would godly men marrying ungodly women produce Nephilim and 'mighty men'? The Sethite view does not explain the offspring.

responses.text: God's people are called his sons and children in many places (Exod 4:22; Deut 14:1; Hos 1:10). The exact phrase is rare, so a handful of uses in Job should not decide its meaning in Genesis.

The contrast is theological: 'sons of God' versus 'daughters of men' means those who belong to God versus those who live merely as humans. That contrast makes sense even if the second phrase is general.
The text does not say the Nephilim were the children; it says they were on the earth then. The children became 'mighty men', famous warriors, which needs no supernatural explanation.

strawMen.strawMan: The Sethite view is a prudish invention to avoid a strange story.
strawMen.correction: It arose from serious reflection on angels' nature and Jesus' words, and from close reading of Gen 4–5.

strawMen.strawMan: It denies that angels or demons exist.
strawMen.correction: Its defenders fully believe in angels and the angelic fall; they simply do not see that fall in Gen 6.

positive: Keeps the focus on human responsibility and the danger of compromise.
Fits the Bible's long concern for the faithfulness of God's people in marriage and community.
negative: Can make the passage a simple lesson on mixed marriage, missing its strangeness.
Has been misused to justify ethnic or tribal separation, which the text does not teach.

positions.name: Ancient kings claiming divine sonship
positions.summary:
This reading sees the 'sons of God' as kings and nobles, rulers who claimed divine descent or divine authority as many ancient monarchs did. 'They took them wives of all which they chose' describes the abuse of royal power: taking any woman they wanted into harems, the kind of oppression shown by Lamech of Cain's line with his two wives and his boast of seventy-sevenfold vengeance (Gen 4:19-24). The 'mighty men' (gibborim) and 'men of renown' are their warrior dynasties, men like Nimrod, 'a mighty one in the earth' (Gen 10:8-9), who make a name for themselves as the builders of Babel later try to do (Gen 11:4).

The reading goes back to second-century rabbinic Judaism. Genesis Rabbah records Rabbi Simeon bar Yohai cursing anyone who called them 'sons of God' (meaning angels) and reading 'sons of judges' or 'nobles'; the Aramaic Targum Onqelos translates 'sons of the great ones', and the Greek translator Symmachus 'sons of the powerful'. In modern scholarship Meredith Kline argued that the sons of God were Cainite kings who claimed divine kingship, and others compare the Epic of Gilgamesh, whose king oppresses his city and takes brides. On this view the passage is about tyranny, violence and the corruption of power, which explains why 'the earth was filled with violence' (Gen 6:11).

positions.context: Rabbis of the second century had reasons to reject the angel story: it was central to apocalyptic and early Christian writings, and it seemed to blame angels for human sin. The 'sons of nobles' reading became standard in rabbinic interpretation and the Targums. Christians largely preferred the Sethite view until the twentieth century, when knowledge of Near Eastern royal ideology (kings as sons of gods in Egypt and Mesopotamia) gave the royal reading new support among scholars such as Kline.
claims: 'Sons of God' refers to kings and nobles who claimed divine sonship or authority.
'Took… all which they chose' describes royal harems and abuse of women by the powerful.
The Nephilim and mighty men are warrior aristocracies, like Nimrod.
The sin is tyranny and violence, which fills the earth before the flood (Gen 6:11).
The passage continues the story of Cain's line, especially Lamech.

scriptures.reading: Lamech takes two wives and boasts of violent revenge: a prototype tyrant.
Nimrod becomes a 'mighty one' (gibbor) in the earth, the same word as Gen 6:4.
The builders of Babel want to 'make us a name', like the 'men of renown' (men of the name).
The earth is filled with violence, the characteristic sin of tyrants.
The king is called God's son, showing royal 'sonship' language.
On one reading, rulers are called 'gods' and 'children of the most High'.

arguments.text: The vocabulary of Gen 6:4 (gibborim, 'name') links to Nimrod and Babel, both stories about power and empire.
The judgement concerns human violence and corruption (Gen 6:11-13), which fits a story about tyrannical rulers.
Near Eastern kings were commonly called sons of gods; in the Epic of Gilgamesh the king oppresses his people and claims brides, a close cultural parallel.
The reading is ancient: it appears in Genesis Rabbah, the Targums and Symmachus, so it is not a modern invention.

critiques.text: No Old Testament passage uses the plural 'sons of God' for kings; the phrase consistently refers to heavenly beings.
Royal polygamy is not obviously the sin that would provoke a universal flood, and the passage does not mention kings or kingship.
The rabbinic reading may have been driven by polemic against apocalyptic and Christian uses of the angel story rather than by the text.

responses.text: Individual kings are called God's son (2 Sam 7:14; Ps 2:7) and rulers can be called elohim; a plural for a royal class is a natural extension, especially in a text using old, compressed language.
The sin is not polygamy alone but violent seizure and the founding of dynasties of oppression, which the text immediately describes as filling the earth with violence.
Motives aside, the reading is supported by internal links to Lamech, Nimrod and Babel that stand on their own.

strawMen.strawMan: This view just explains away the supernatural.
strawMen.correction: Its defenders believe in angels; they argue the passage is about the abuse of human power, a deeply theological theme.

strawMen.strawMan: It says the Nephilim were ordinary people.
strawMen.correction: It says they were feared warrior elites, the most powerful men of their age.

positive: Highlights the Bible's critique of tyranny, violence and abuse of women by the powerful.
Connects Genesis 6 with the themes of Cain, Nimrod and Babel.
negative: Can seem to read Near Eastern parallels into a short text.
Has fewer explicit biblical parallels for the plural phrase than the other views.

readings.reading: 'Sons of God' (bene ha-elohim) elsewhere in the Hebrew Bible means heavenly beings (Job 1:6; Job 2:1; Job 38:7). Heavenly beings crossed the boundary between heaven and earth and took human wives.
The 'sons of God' are the line of Seth, who 'called upon the name of the LORD' (Gen 4:26). They chose wives for beauty from the ungodly line of Cain, and godliness collapsed.

The 'sons of God' are kings and nobles who, like Near Eastern rulers, claimed divine sonship. 'They took… all which they chose' describes royal harems and abuse of power, following the polygamous tyrant Lamech (Gen 4:19-24).
The Nephilim are the giant offspring of angels and women, the 'mighty men… of renown' of ancient legend. 'And also after that' allows for later giant clans.
The Nephilim were violent, powerful men who were already on the earth; the text does not say they were the children of the marriages. The offspring became famous warriors, not hybrids.

The Nephilim and 'mighty men' (gibborim) are a warrior aristocracy like Nimrod, 'a mighty one in the earth' (Gen 10:8-9). 'Men of renown' (literally 'men of the name') are tyrants making a name for themselves, as at Babel (Gen 11:4).
The same phrase, 'sons of God', clearly means heavenly beings presenting themselves before God. This is the closest parallel and should decide Gen 6.
Job is a different book with a heavenly setting; in Genesis the context is the human genealogies of Gen 4–5. Believers are also called God's sons elsewhere (Deut 14:1; Hos 1:10).
Job shows the phrase can mean heavenly beings, but kings could also be called God's sons (2 Sam 7:14; Ps 2:7) and rulers 'gods' (on one reading of Ps 82:6). Context must decide.

Angels who 'left their own habitation' are kept in chains; 'even as Sodom and Gomorrha… in like manner' went after 'strange flesh'. This links the angels' sin to sexual transgression, exactly as in 1 Enoch, which Jude quotes (Jude 1:14-15).
Jude speaks of an angelic fall, probably the original rebellion, and 'in like manner' may compare Sodom with the cities around it, not with the angels. Jude does not mention Gen 6.
Jude uses a well-known Jewish tradition as an illustration of judgement on rebels. Using a tradition as an example does not settle what Gen 6 originally meant.
Peter places the angels' sin and their imprisonment in Tartarus right next to the flood, matching the order of Gen 6 and the Enoch tradition.
Peter gives a sequence of judgements (angels, flood, Sodom) without saying that the angels' sin was marrying women; it can refer to the original angelic fall.
Peter's 'Tartarus' and imprisoned angels echo popular Jewish tradition; he is warning false teachers, not commenting on Genesis.
Jesus says angels 'in heaven' do not marry, describing their proper state, not what rebellious angels who left heaven could do (Jude 1:6).
Angels do not marry, so the sons of God must be human. Augustine and many Reformers found this decisive.
Supports a human reading. Angels do not marry; kings with harems certainly do.

The Anakim are linked to the Nephilim, so giant clans survived or reappeared after the flood ('and also after that', Gen 6:4), explaining the Rephaim, Og (Deut 3:11) and Goliath. Some defenders add that the spies may have exaggerated, since this was an 'evil report' (Num 13:32).
All the Nephilim died in the flood. The spies use 'Nephilim' as a legendary name for terrifying giants, part of an 'evil report' (Num 13:32) meant to frighten Israel.
'Nephilim' had become a byword for fearsome warrior peoples. The frightened spies used it of the tall Anakim, just as people call a tyrant 'a Nero'.

timeline.note: Justin's *Second Apology* 5 says angels fell through love of women and fathered demons; Athenagoras and Irenaeus say similar things.

timeline.title: Rabbi Simeon bar Yohai
timeline.note: Genesis Rabbah 26:5 records him cursing those who call them 'sons of God' and reading 'sons of judges/nobles'. Targum Onqelos has 'sons of the great ones'.

timeline.title: Julius Africanus
timeline.note: His *Chronographiai* (preserved in fragments) offers the Sethite reading as preferable, while noting copies that read 'angels of God'.

timeline.title: Augustine
timeline.note: *City of God* 15.23 argues at length for the Sethite view; it becomes the standard Western reading.

timeline.title: Calvin on Genesis
timeline.note: Calvin calls the angelic view absurd and reads the sons of God as the godly line; Luther also held a Sethite view.

timeline.title: Kline's 'Divine Kingship'
timeline.note: Meredith Kline argues in the Westminster Theological Journal that the sons of God were Cainite kings claiming divine status.

timeline.title: Modern revival of the angelic view
timeline.note: Gordon Wenham's Genesis commentary and many critical scholars return to a divine-beings reading; Michael Heiser's *Reversing Hermon* (2017) popularises it.

influence.note: The rabbinic 'sons of nobles' reading arose partly as a reaction against the angel story and its use in apocalyptic and Christian circles.
The Sethite reading was proposed as an alternative to angels who marry, which seemed to contradict Jesus' teaching and angelic nature.
Kline and others kept the Sethite view's human focus but replaced the godly line with a royal Cainite line.

argumentMap.text: The sons of God were angels who married women and fathered the Nephilim.
Elsewhere 'sons of God' always means heavenly beings.
Jude and 2 Peter link fallen, imprisoned angels with sexual sin and the flood.
It is the oldest recorded interpretation and the view of most early Fathers.
Angels do not marry.
Jesus speaks of angels in heaven; these angels abandoned their proper dwelling.
The judgement falls on humans, not angels, which suits a human sin.
The sons of God were the godly line of Seth marrying ungodly women.
Genesis 4–5 sets the line of Cain against the line of Seth, who called on the LORD.
God's people are called his sons, and mixed marriage is a constant biblical warning.
'Daughters of men' in 6:1 means all human daughters; switching to 'Cainite women' in 6:2 is unsignalled.
The contrast between 'God' and 'men' is the point: those who belong to God join themselves to those who do not.
The sons of God were kings claiming divine sonship who seized wives and founded warrior dynasties.
Kings could be called God's son, and ancient rulers claimed divine descent.
Lamech's polygamy and violence and Nimrod as a 'mighty one' fit the pattern of tyranny.
No Old Testament text calls a group of kings 'sons of God' in the plural; the phrase is used for heavenly beings.
The singular royal usage and Near Eastern parallels make a plural 'sons of the gods' for a royal class plausible; context, not word count, must decide.
The angelic view rests on Second Temple legends that the canonical texts only allude to.
